Chapter 2 - Character Creation
Leveling Up as a Trainer
As you proceed on your Journey as a Trainer, you will 
gain Merits, which serve as Experience Points for your 
Character .
PTE follows a Psuedo-Milestone level based 
progression system, so whenever the GM narratively 
feels  as  though  a  goal  has  been  accomplished  they 
grant Merits to the Party based on the impact of the 
Milestone.
Whenever the Party reaches the Merits Needed in the 
chart below, they reset to 0 Merits and Level up!
We  reccommend  that  whenever  the  Party  is  at  the 
Level on the Left, they need the following amount of 
Merits  to  advance  to  the  next  Level,  however, based 
on your preference you can adjust how fast they level 
up. For example if you want a slower paced Campaign, 
they could need 5 Merits from Level 1-5 to Level up.  
Trainers usually  all  start  at  Level 1   and  can  reach  a 
Maximum of Level 20. At Trainer Level 1, apply all of 
the following benefits to your Trainer!
At Level 1 you start with...

•  4 Features

•  2 Talents

•  1 Adept Rank Skill, 3 Novice Rank Skills,  
and 3 Pathetic Skills

•  +10 Level-Up Stat Points to Distribute

•  Base Stats as a Trainer of 10 HP , and 5 in  
every other Stat
After this point, each time your Trainer levels up, they 
gain the following benefits listed below. Follow this list 
to  determine  what  your  Trainer gets  everytime  they 
Level Up. 
Each Level-Up

•  You gain a Class Feature or General Feature

•  You rank up a Skill or gain a Talent 

•  You gain +5 Level-Up Stat Points to Distribute. 
  [Remember the Glass Cannon Rule]

•  Your Maximum Pokemon Level increases by +5 

•  Your Pokemon increase their Level by up to +5
Specific Level Milestones
At  Level  5,  10  and  15,  you  gain  and  unlock  certain 
Milestones which are listed below!

• At Level 5 -   You gain +10  Level-Up  Stat Points and 
qualify to take Expert Rank Skills

• At Level 10 - You qualify to take Master Rank Skills

• At Level 15 -  You gain +10 Level-Up Stat Points and 
qualify to take Virtuoso Rank Skills
In addition, at each of the Levels listed abov e,  you 
may  choose  one  of  the  following  bonuses  to  gain  as 
well:

•  You learn the Skill Specialty Talent 

•  Choose two Skills that are Novice Rank or below to 
Rank up. At Level 10 & 15 you may instead choose two 
Skills that are Adept Rank or below to Rank up.
Trainer Progression
Party Level Merits Needed
Level 1-5 3
Level 6-10 5
Level 11-15 7
Level 16-20 10

title: Chapter 2 - Character Creation (p.26)
body:
2626
Chapter 2 - Character Creation
26
Major Milestones - 3 Merits
Major Milestones are given out when a pillar of your 
Campaign has been completed. These should usually be 
clear before a Campaign begins on what quantifies as a 
Major Milestone. For a Gym Crawl, a Major Milestone 
is defeating a Gym. For Dragonball Z, finding one of the 
7 dragon balls is a Major Milestone, etc. 
Example (Gym Campaign) -  The Players go to Cerulean City 
and spend the next session preparing for and eventually 
defeating Misty. This counts as one of their 8 Gym Badges 
and they are granted with 3 Merits. 
Example (Conquest Campaign) - The Players are reclaiming 
cities that are overtaken with Shadow Pokemon. After 
defeating a big Guardian Boss and the pack dispursing, they 
save the town and gain 3 Merits. 
Example (Narrative Campaign) -  The Party has a big 
confrontation with an Admin of Team Rocket with the goal 
being taking down Giovanni from within. 
Legendary Milestones - 5 Merits
Legendary  Milestones  are  pivotal  moments  in  your 
Campaign that defy the odds. These should rarely be 
given out but if your Party succeeded something truly 
difficult, they should be rewarded in kind with 5 Merits.   
Example (Defeating a Legendary) -  The Party is called on a 
mission to reclaim an island that is being overan by minions 
controlled by Pecharunt. After a few sessions they finally 
encounter the Legendary and defeat it!
Example (Defeating the Elite Four) -  Nearing the end 
of their Journey, the Party challenges the Elite Four and 
becomes Champions, moving the Campaign into the end 
game zone where they roam the region and challenge 
bigger bosses. 
Example (Beating a major NPC) -  The Party confronts 
Giovanni and ambushes him with a group of police, ready 
to arrest him. A major confrontation happens and against 
all odds, the players succeed!
Simple Milestones - 1 Merit
The simplest of milestones should only grant 1 Merit. 
These  tend  to  be  either  easy  missions  or  above  and 
beyond successes that a Player performs, allowing you 
to give chip exp as a reward. If you’re impressed with 
how the Players dealt with an encounter, grant them a 
bonus Merit! Not all Encounters or battles qualify as a 
Simple Milestone. 
Example (Simple Quest) -  The Players are asked to go clear 
some Rattata that are frequently stealing from a Pokemart’s 
storage facilities. They go to the storage and defeat them 
in battle, rewarding them 1 Merit alongside other rewards 
offered by the shopkeep.
Example (Notable Success) -  The GM is impressed after 
a Level 2 Trainer manages to trick a Nidoking into leaving 
their party alone after they have their Zorua conjure an 
Illusion of a Tyranitar .
Example (Notable Success) -  The GM is impressed after 
the Party successfully convinces a group of cultist Pokemon 
to abandon their ritual in favor of helping the community. 
Notable Milestones - 2 Merits
Notable  Milestones  are  basically  a  Simple  Milestone 
in  scope,  but  it  was  mechanically  harder  or  more 
time consuming than normal. It doesn’t need to have 
the same impact as a Major Milestone but if it was a 
difficult  scenario,  grant  2  Merits.  Notable  Milestones 
are  usually  a  difficult  task  that  works  towards  the 
greater scheme of the Campaign. 
Example (Harder Quest) -  The Party is planning a heist of 
Professor Oak’s lab and spend the session preparing for it. 
The heist itself is fairly challenging with multiple obstacles 
and Pokemon to face but they succeed and gain 2 Merits!
Example (Defeating an important NPC) -  The Party comes 
across the admin of Team Magma and is ambushed into 
a battle. This is certainly more difficult than your everday 
trainer and they have to deal with threats on all sides. 
After defeating the admin and escaping however, they’re 
rewarded with 2 Merits. 
Gaining Merits
As you progress in your Campaign and accomplish tasks as the heroes, your Party will gain Merits over time and level 
up. The below section notes how many Merits you tend to gain based on the Milestone you completed and can be a 
rough guide on how the GM can distribute EXP . 
Example (Leveling Up) - A Party is at 2 Merits and is Level 3 and 
they manage to defeat the Pewter City Gym! This is a Major 
Milestone for a Gym Crawl Campaign so the Party gains 3 Merits. 
This lets them Level Up immediately, then sets them to 2 Merits 
again, since they only need 3 to Level Up at this stage.

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
body:
2727
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
27
Now you should have your Character created! So let’s overview 
each aspect that makes your Character who they are.
Talents
Talents are almost always non-Mechanical aspects that support 
a Character’s non-combat utility. Talents could grant effects such 
as being able to see in the dark, being able to speak to pokemon, 
allowing them to craft specific items or allowing them to use 
Skills in more versatile manners.  
General Features
General Features that allow Trainers to become better in 
mechanical aspects of the system but not good enough 
to specialize in it. These grant Players tools that should be 
accessible regardless of the classes taken by the Player, such as 
learning Attacks or Orders. 
Classes
Other than General Features, there are also Class Features 
which are bundled into a group known as a Class. Classes are 
small pools of mechanical effects that are focused on improving 
combat capabilities around a certain idea. For example, the 
Berserker Class will grant you tools to mechanically become an 
enraged warrior and live out the trope. The first Feature in each 
Class has a [Class] Tag, and you can only have 4 of these Features 
in total, thereby, you can only benefit from features from 4 
Classes per Character . 
Classes have two Categories, [Base] and [Advanced]. [Base] 
Classes tend to have generic tools that support a playstyle of 
your choice, while [Advanced] Classes tend to be more specific 
in how the associated playstyle is expressed. All Fighters are 
good at punching Pokemon but Berserkers specialize in doing so 
while enraged.   
Note -  GMs should be wary of Characters that take multiple 
[Advanced] Classes from the same [Base] Class. These builds tend to 
be way more synergistic, minmaxy and lead to builds that are hyper 
specific but not versatile. It used to be a rule of only having 1 Advanced 
Class from a root [Base] but we will instead have that be a home rule 
where GMs can ban certain combos like stacking tons of Damage 
Reduction from Defender Classes. 
Pokemon
Of course, a Pokemon Trainer is also defined by the Pokemon 
they train and own. Each Player can carry up to 3 Pokemon at 
a time to consist of their Party, but can own and train as many 
as they want! And the leveling system is simple enough where 
Pokemon don’t have to undergo grinding or sit in the box for 
ages before they can be used. 
Aspects of a Character

title: Gladiator
body:
Gladiator
[Class][Advanced]
Prerequisite 1: Fighter or Provocateur [or] 
Prerequisite 2: Adept Combat and Novice Charm or Command
At-Will - Free Action
Trigger: You Provoke an Enemy, an Attack misses you or you cause an Enemy to faint with an Attack.
Effect: You gain +1 Glory Counter (Max 6). For each Glory Counter you have, you have a +1 Modifier 
to Accuracy for Melee Attacks. Whenever you Faint or at the end of the Scene, you lose all Glory 
Counters. Whenever your Pokemon Faint, you lose half of your Glory Counters (Rounded Down).
Bonus: You learn the Taunt Attack.
Note: If you provoke or faint multiple enemies with the same instance, you only get 1 Counter.
2828
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Understanding PTE Text
Gladiator is an At-Will Feature that can be used as a Free 
Action. Frequencies you will see on Features are as follows:

• At-Will - These Features have no restriction on how often they can  
be used

• Static -   These  Features  are  always  in  effect  and  treated  as 
“Passives” .

• Scene x Y - This means you can only use the Feature Y amount 
of times during the Scene. If [x Y] isn’t shown, it can only be used 
once per Scene.

• Bind X - These Features may be bound to a number of Targets 
equal to X.  Each time this Feature is  used,  you must choose  a 
new Target to Bind its effects to. Whenever a Target is bound, 
it persists even after a Scene is completed and carries into new 
Scenes.
Conditions  that  are  listed  must  be  true  in  order  to  use 
Effect. 
Targets specify what Combatants the Effect will apply to. 
Triggers specify what needs to happen in order to use this 
Effect and  cannot  be  used  otherwise.  Triggers can  only 
lead  to  one  activation  per  instance,  so  even  if  multiple 
requirements of a condition are met, it can only activate 
once. Effects that have a Trigger attached are able to be used 
when  it  isn’t  the  user’s Turn. Triggers occur  immediately 
once  their  condition  is  met,  and  the  interrupted  action 
does  not  resume  until  the  Trigger’s Effect is  resolved.  If 
you  do  not  have  an  available  Action  that  is  required  for 
the Effect to activate, it cannot be Triggered. For instance, 
if I already used my Trainer’s Reaction this Round, I cannot 
Trigger the Attack of Opportunity Maneuver again until the 
start of the next Round. 
The  Effect  determines  its  details  and  what  it  does  upon 
activation. Attack Effects always occur  after the  Attack is 
resolved, unless stated otherwise.
The Bonus line in a Feature is an additional Effect, however 
it is always treated as a Static Frequency and is separated 
from the main effect and activations of the feature. 
The  Name  is  simply  the  name  of  the  Feature.  When 
performing data entry for your Trainer, this name will pull 
up all of its information
The Tags convey the information about the Feature. The 
following Feature Tags that you will find are listed below.

• [Class] -   You can  only  have  4  Features with  the  [Class]  Tag. 
[Class]  Features  are  always  the  first  feature  in  a  Class,  which 
qualifies you to take further Features in that Class! 

• [Base] -Some Classes will have the [Base] Tag. This Tag is to 
signify that this Class is designed around a general playstyle and 
its  features grant tools  to  support  that  concept. These  classes 
are  also  one  method  of  qualifying  for  [Adv}  Classes,  such  as 
taking Marksman which qualifies you to take the Sniper Class. 

• [Advanced] - Advanced Classes are meant to be specialized in 
design around a specific concept based on one of their [Base] 
Classes. This Tag and [Base] are tags notifying its category and 
hierarchy, not having any mechanical distinction or restrictions 
of its own.

• [Order] - Orders can only be given while the User is able to 
communicate with  their  Target.  They  may be  used  as  if  it  had 
the Priority Keyword, letting it be used after any Action resolves. 

• [Ranked X] - Features with the Ranked Tag may be taken up to 
X times. Each time you take a new rank, follow the Effect under 
that  Rank.  In  order  to  meet  the  prerequisites  for  each  Rank, 
you  must  have  taken the  previous  Ranks  and  meet  any  listed 
Prerequisite under  that  specific  Rank.  Each  Rank  is  treated  as 
a different Feature, for the sake of  needing X  amount of Class 
Features, for example. 
 
The Prerequisites lists the minimum requirements needed 
to take the Feature. If there are two sets of Prerequisites, 
you only need to meet one in order to take it, so in order 
to take the Gladiator Feature, you need either the Fighter 
Feature  or  at  least  Adept  Combat  and  at  least  Novice 
Charm  or  Command.  (If  you  have  Master  Combat,  you 
qualify because you exceed the Prerequisites)
The Frequency / Action of a Feature lists how often you 
can use this Feature and what Action it takes to activate it. 
Features, Orders and Traits are a large mechanical basis of your Character, and as such you should learn how to read 
and comprehend them! Below is an example of a Feature that has been labeled 
NAME
TAGS
FREQ.

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.29)
body:
Example (Skill Check)- Theo the Ranger was sent on a mission to track a child that 
went missing in the forest a week ago and hasn’t returned. He heads out to the 
woods and is asked to perform a Perception or Nature Edu Check. He is told that the 
Challenge Rating will be Standard, meaning he needs 2 Successes in order to pass. 
He performs a Nature Edu Check. He currently has Adept Rank so he rolls a 4 d 6. His 
results are 3,5,4,2, resulting in two Successes. The GM informs Theo that through his 
knowledge of tracking in the wild, he notices some footprints that seem fresh going in 
a specific direction.
2929
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Skills
Pokemon Skills
Similar  to  Trainers,  Pokemon  also  have  Skills,  albeit 
they have different Ranks and names when compared 
to  Trainers. Considering  Skills  potency  should  change 
upon evolution, they’re separated into 4 Ranks.
Inept - The First and second Stage of a 3 Stage Pokemon 
or the first stage of a 2 Stage Pokemon has 1 d 6 in an 
Inept Skill. The last Evolution of any Pokemon has 2 d 6. 
Inept Skills cannot be increased by any means. 
Untrained -  The  first  and  second  stage  of  a  3  Stage 
Pokemon  or  the  first  stage  of  a  2  Stage  Pokemon 
has  2 d 6  in  this  Skill.  The  last  Evolution  Stage  of  any 
Pokemon has 3 d 6. 
Proficient -  The  first stage of  a  3  Stage Pokemon has 
3 d 6 in this Skill. The second stage in a 3 Stage Pokemon 
or the first stage of a 2 Stage Pokemon has 4 d 6. The last 
Evolution Stage of any Pokemon has 5 d 6. 
Mastered -  The  first stage of  a  3  Stage Pokemon has 
4 d 6 in this Skill. The second stage in a 3 Stage Pokemon 
or the first stage of a 2 Stage Pokemon has 5 d 6. The last 
Evolution Stage of any Pokemon has 6 d 6. 
Skill Categories
Skills  are  divided  into  3  Categories  for  the  sake  of 
organization. They aren’t referenced often but can be 
used for quick reference of what they affect. 
Ex: A Player is sleepy so their Body Skills have a penalty.
Body - Acrobatics, Athletics, Combat, Intimidate, Stealth
Spirit  -  Charm,  Command,  Focus,  Guile,  Intuition, 
Perception
Knowledge -  Gen  Edu,  Med  Edu,  Nature  Edu,  Occult 
Edu, Poke Edu, Tech Edu
 
The  Attributes  of  your  Trainer  and  what  they’re 
good at is measured in what are known as Skills and 
Skill Ranks. Skills  represent  a  Character’s  conscious 
interest, training and are used to measure if someone 
is successful at a task through Skill Checks. When you 
perform a Skill Check, refer to the value listed next to 
your corresponding Skill Rank and that’ll be how many 
d 6’s  your  dice  pool  consists  of.  (More  info  on  Skill 
Checks will be in that section) 
There are 7 Ranks of Skills , each rank causing you to 
roll a different number of dice when performing a Skill 
Check.  At Character Creation,   all  Trainers start  with 
their Skills at Untrained (Rank 2), which at Level 1 they 
adjust 3 to Novice (Rank 3), 1 to Adept (Rank 4) and 3 
to Pathetic (Rank 1). 
Every level-up beyond that, you’re able to forgo taking 
a  Talent to improve the  Rank  of  one  of  your Skills  by 
one  Rank.  The  only  Skill  Rank  that  deviates from  the 
standard rule is Virtuoso Rank, which is the same Dice 
Pool as Master Rank. Whenever perform a Skill Check 
with a Virtuoso Skill, you always gain a Boon towards 
the roll. However, you can only have one Skill with the 
Virtuoso Rank.
The  last  rule  regarding  Skill  Ranks  is  that all Ranks 
above Adept have a Minimum Level Requirement in 
before it can be Ranked Up. In order to Rank Up a Skill 
to Expert Rank, you need to be at least Trainer Level 5. 
In order to Rank up a Skill to Master Rank, you need 
to be  at least Level 10.  In  order to Rank  up  a  Skill  to 
Virtuoso Rank, you need to be at least Level 15. 
Rank # Rank Name Dice Roll
1 Pathetic 1 d 6
2 Untrained 2 d 6
3 Novice 3 d 6
4 Adept 4 d 6
5 Expert 5 d 6
6 Master 6 d 6
6 Virtuoso 6 d 6
Example (Pokemon Skills) -  A Charmander has Proficient Combat 
which means it rolls a 3 d 6. A Scizor with Proficient Combat rolls 
5 d 6. Scyther with Proficient Combat rolls 4 d 6. Why? Charmander 
is the first stage of a 3 Stage Line (Charmander , Charmeleon, 
Charizard). Scyther is the first stage in a 2 Stage Line (Scyther, 
Scizor). And Scizor is the last stage of an evolution line.

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.30)
body:
3030
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Focus

•  Your ability to concentrate on high precision tasks or 
when distracted

•  Your ability to perform while distracted or in a high 
stress situation

•  Your ability to be precise and accurate
Ex 1: A Trainer is lockpicking a fairly sturdy and advanced lock
Ex 2: A Mime Jr . is trying to hold concentration to the invisible 
walls it made
Guile

•  Your ability to lie, deceive and manipulate others

•  Your ability to control your body language and 
expressions

•  Your ability to improvise and use your wit to plan
Ex 1: A Trainer comes up with an idea to hide amongst a crowd 
when escaping enemies
Ex 2: A Trainer lies to a guard when they didn’t have a permit 
to enter the city.
Intimidate

•  Your ability to be convincing in a fearful manner

•  Your ability to scare or impose your presence on others

•  The level of physical or psychological fear you can inflict
Ex 1: A Trainer attempts to scare off a hostile mimikyu
Ex 2: A Trainer is interrogating a prisoner and demands 
information and threatens them
Intuition

•  Your sensation of instinct and gut feeling to analyze 
surroundings 

•  Your ability to analyze information and gain insight

•  Your ability to discern if something abnormal in a non-
physical sense such as behavioral
Ex 1: A Trainer can tell something is off when an NPC is 
attempting to lie to them
Ex 2: A Trainer can sense a disturbance in Pokemon around 
them from an ambush nearby 
Athletics

•  Your ability to perform feats of strength and 
endurance

•  Your level of physical fitness, health and immunity
Ex 1: A Trainer is trying to lift a fairly large boulder
Ex 2: A Trainer is trying to see how many beers they can 
drink before they get drunk
Acrobatics

•  Your ability to be nimble and fleet footed

•  Your ability to perform precise footwork or  
be swift
Ex 1: A Trainer is attempting to jump across a roof in a 
pursuit
Ex 2: A Trainer is running through the city and would trip on 
a crate
Charm

•  Your ability to soothe and calm others 

•  Your ability to be convincing in a persuasive manner

•  The level of physical or psychological attractiveness 
you can express at will or naturally
Ex 1: A Trainer is trying to console a crying Teddiursa that 
lost its mom
Ex 2: A Trainer is trying to get information by flirting with a 
bartender 
Combat

•  Your ability to perform tactics in a battle

•  Your knowledge on battle tactics and how factors 
would affect combat
Ex 1: A Trainer is attempting to gauge what an enemy may 
do next in battle
Ex 2: A Trainer wants to know which attack may deal more 
damage to a heavily armored enemy
Command

•  Your ability to lead, order and inspire others

•  Your ability to be convincing in an authoritative 
manner
Ex 1: A Trainer orders a wild Pokemon to assist them in a jail 
break
Ex 2: A Trainer speaks to a crowd trying to instill a rebellion
Skill List
Below is a list of each Skill, what it controls and enables your Character to be good at, and an example of an Occasion 
where it’d be requested for a Skill Check. 
As a GM, remember that there are some facets of Skills that a Character could be weaker in. Especially for skills like 
Occult Education, a Trainer may excel in witchcraft but have no knowledge of artificing that isn’t common knowledge, 
despite being under the same skill umbrella. A Character could have a high Combat Rank due to theoretical battle 
tactics, but be bad at performing maneuvers. This nuance could be factored into Skill Checks by being given a Bane, 
for example.

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.31)
body:
3131
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
31
Nature Education [Nature Edu]

•  Your knowledge of nature, flora and ecosystems

•  Your knowledge of undomesticated  
wild Pokemon

•  Your ability to survive in the wild or perform 
activities in the nature
Ex 1: A Trainer recognizes that this cluster of mushroom are 
indeed poisonous
Ex 2: A Trainer recalls on how to start a campfire in the 
middle of the woods to set up camp
Occult Education [Occult Edu]

•  Your knowledge on any supernatural or mystical 
subject unique to your setting
Ex 1: This can include magical forces of reality, religion, 
mythical forces or ghosts.
Ex 2: A Trainer recognizes material used for a ritual to 
summon Darkrai
Ex 3: A Trainer is aware of the history of Moltres and the 
past Trainers that commanded it
Pokemon Education [Poke Edu]

•  Your Knowledge on Pokemon Biology, Behaviors and 
their Habitats

•  Your ability to interact with Pokemon
Ex 1: A Trainer is observing foot prints and recognizes it is a 
Mightyena 
Ex 2: A Trainer remembers that Scrafty bond by being 
mischievous together rather than charming and social.
Technology Education [Tech Edu]

•  Your ability to understand, manipulate or create 
Technology unique to your setting
Ex 1: A Trainer is reviewing a security camera system to see 
if they can delete footage
Ex 2: A Trainer wishes to hack a Villain’s Pokeball in order to 
release the Pokemon they stole
Perception

•  Your awareness and attentiveness of your 
surroundings

•  Your ability to discern details and if something is 
physically abnormal

•  Your ability to see with clarity further distances
Ex 1: A Trainer notices a strange marking on the armor of a 
Golurk, like an insignia
Ex 2: A Trainer spots a Kecleon that is attempting to ambush 
the party in hiding 
Stealth

•  Your ability to stay undetected from others

•  Your ability to perform sleight of hand
Ex 1: A Trainer attempts to pickpocket a passerby while 
their friend talks to them
Ex 2: A Trainer is performing a magic trick and doesn’t want 
the trick to be discovered
General Education [Gen Edu]

•  Your ability to recall knowledge that doesn’t fall 
under any other category

•  Your knowledge on History, Cultural or Geographical 
Information
Ex 1: A Trainer recalls information on a war in Kalos
Ex 2: A Trainer remembers information about a famous 
mafia boss in Kanto
Medicine Education [Med Edu]

•  Your ability to understand the anatomy and biology 
of living creatures

•  Your ability to use medicinal items and perform 
medical procedures

•  Your ability to discern afflictions and ailments and 
how to treat them
Ex 1: A Trainer is able to use medical tools to bandage a 
gash on a nidorino
Ex 2: A Trainer is able to treat a burn wound on their ally 
without it causing worse damage

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.32)
body:
3232
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Skill Checks
Basic Skill Check 
Basic Skill Checks are when a Character interacts with 
a  non-Character  entity  that  has  a  static  difficulty. 
Alternatively this could be a Character entity that isn’t 
opposing  you  or  contesting  your  attempt.  This  can 
include  attempting  to  recall  information,  attempting 
to break down a door or trying to navigate precarious 
terrain! 
Ex: James is attempting to scavenge for some plants that can 
create dye he needs for a disguise. The GM determines the 
CR  is  Simple,  considering the  area he  went to is  abundant 
with them. They also set the Skill to either be Perception or 
Nature Edu of their choice. James uses his Untrained Rank 
Perception, rolling a 1 and 4, thus passing the check. 
Opposed Skill Check 
Opposed  Skill  Checks  are  always  when  a  Character 
interacts with another living entity that can oppose the 
Character’s attempts. When choosing this, pick which 
Skill(s) will be used to perform the task and which will 
be used to oppose the task. Then, count the number 
of  Successes  on  each  side.  Whichever  side  has  more 
Successes wins the opposed check. If they have equal 
Successes, instead, add the value of all rolled die and 
whichever is higher wins the check. 
Ex: James is attempting to pickpocket a merchant while they 
talk to a customer . It will be a Stealth Roll (Expert) opposed 
by the Merchant’s Perception (Adept). James rolls a 4,2,5,3,3 
resulting in 2 Successes. The merchant rolls 4,2,3,1 resulting 
in 1 Success. James wins this Opposed Check.
Group Skill Check 
Group Skill  Checks  are  Skill  Checks  that  involve all  or 
at least 3+ Characters performing the same task, each 
having the ability to fail. When performing this, take the 
Challenge Rating, then add to it equal to the number 
of Characters participating in this check. All Characters 
will then perform the Skill Check and the group counts 
their total Successes.
Ex: James and his gang of 3 grunts attempt to sneak through 
a town hall while a ceremony is going on. It is deemed to be 
a Stealth Check with a CR of Tough. There are 4 Characters so 
the Tough Challenge (3) plus the Characters (4) equal a total 
CR of 7. The group all rolls and gets a total of 5 Successes, 
leading to a failure and they’re spotted by a waitress. 
Luck Check 
A Luck Check is something that is the opposite of Skill 
Checks.  Whenever  you  want  randomness  in  a  result, 
perform this. To do so, simply roll a d 20. The GM will 
set a range of outcomes depending on the task. A 3 or 
less  is  usually  a  very bad  result. A  4-10  is  an  average 
result.  11-16  is  a  good  result.  A  17+  is  a  very  good 
result. And a 20+ is a very lucky result! These are also 
known as Luck Rolls.  
For  this  section,  let’s  say  we  have  a  rogue  Trainer 
who  is  a  part  of  team  rocket named  James.  In  order 
to  determine  how  James  succeeds  or  fails  when 
interacting with  the  world,  he’ll  perform  Skill  Checks 
that  test  his  capabilities,  each  of  which  having  a 
Challenge Rating (CR) which means he needs an equal 
or greater number of successes than the CR to  beat 
the Skill Check. 
By default, all die results of 4 or higher are counted as 
1 Success. (This can be adjusted with Boons & Banes). 
However, any results of 6 are counted as 2 Successes 
instead of 1!
There are multiple types of Skill Checks that a GM can 
choose from listed below, and when decided, the GM 
will  also  set  its  CR,  determine  any  Boons  or  Banes, 
then they’ll list all Skills that are applicable for this Skill 
Check. Once this is done, the Player will roll their dice 
pool  for  the  relevant  Skill  and  count  the  number  of 
successes to see if they beat the CR.
Ex:  If  a  Player  has  Adept  Occult  Edu  and  is  looking  at  an 
artifact to gauge its  origins,  they’ll  roll a  4 d 6.  The  check  is 
deemed to be Tough CR (3). They roll a 6,4,4,1. This results in 
4 Successes and they pass
Below  is  a  step by  step list of  questions to  ask  when 
creating a Skill Check:
1. What Type of Skill Check is it?
Listed below  there are multiple  types  of  Skill  Checks, 
including Basic, Opposed, Group or Luck Checks.
2. How difficult is the Skill Check
There are 6 levels of difficulty, listed in the Challenge 
Rating  section.  These  levels  are  Trivial, Standard, 
Tough, Severe, Extreme and Nearly Impossible .  The 
Challenge Rating will  determine how  many successes 
the Character needs in order to pass the check.
3. What Skills can be used for this Task?
Oftentimes  multiple  Skill  can  apply  to  a  single  skill 
check so negotiate with the table on what would make 
most sense.
4. What happens on a Success or Failure?
The GM will finally decide what occurs based on how 
many Successes they got compared to how many were 
needed. 
1 Success 2 Successes
4 Successes

title: Challenge Ratings
body:
3333
Challenge Ratings
There are 6 Levels of Difficulty a task can be, known as the Challenge Rating of a Skill Check (Abbreviated as CR), 
listed below. 
Below  are  some  examples  of  Scenarios  in  which  a 
Skill Check is used and their corresponding Challenge 
Ratings. 
Example (Basic Check) :  James  prepares  a  disguise  as  a 
server  at  a  wedding.  He  rolls  a  Guile  Check  vs  the  initial 
wave  of  employees  to  gain  entry  without  suspicion.  The 
GM determines this to be easy with a Trivial CR (1). This is 
due to his disguise being convincing so they wouldn’t have a 
reason to be suspicious immediately. He has an Adept Guile 
and rolls, resulting in a 3,4,2,1, leading to 1 Success and he 
passes  the  Check.  He  gets  a  few glances  but  nobody  calls 
him out on it. 
Example (Opposed Check) :  James  then  runs  into  a 
supervisor who doesn’t recognize him as working there. He 
lies and says he’s covering someone else’s shift, resulting in 
an opposed Guile vs Intuition Check. James has a flaw that 
he’s gets nervous when he lies but his Guile is good because 
he’s great at disguises. This results in his check being made 
with a Bane. The Manager also has Expert Intuition. James 
rolls a 4,5,3,1 resulting in one success because of the Bane. 
The  Manager  also  has  a  Bane  since  James  has  a  Disguise 
equipped and they’re trying to discern his identity, then he 
rolls  a  4,2,4,1,6,  resulting  in  two  successes.  The  Manager 
wins the opposed check and gets suspicious, calling him out. 
Example (Negotiating a Check): James decides to run away 
through the  kitchen and  halls  of  the  palace,  attempting to 
find  a  hiding  spot  where  he  can  lose  the  supervisor . The 
area has a lot of places to hide so the CR would be Standard 
(2), but considering he’s panicking, he’ll have a Bane to this 
Perception or  Stealth  Check.  The  Player asks  the  GM  if  he 
can perform a Focus Check to remove the Bane, which he 
passes,  allowing  James  to  calm  down  for a  second  to  find 
a hiding spot. He has an Adept Stealth, which he rolls and 
results in a 4,2,5,3, being 2 Successes, finding a cabinet he 
could  lose  the  Manager . If  the  Bane  wasn’t  removed,  he 
would have failed this check!
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Challenge 
Rating
# of Successes 
Needed Skill Checks of this CR...
Trivial 1+ …Are relatively easy but can be messed up by someone 
who has no clue what they’re doing or is being careless.
Standard 2+ …Require a minimum level of competence or a bit of luck 
to accomplish.
Tough 3+ …Are very difficult for someone without experience but is 
a fairly typical task for someone with it.
Severe 4+
…Are anything that someone without experience would 
have no clue how to complete. Even with training, it would 
be difficult and can sometimes fail.
Extreme 5+ …Are only achievable by or with the assistance of 
individuals that are very talented in this Skill.
Nearly Impossible 8+ … Are the toughest of tasks, even for those who are well 
versed in this Skill.
The Challenge Rating depends on the inherent difficulty 
of the task. If context involving the Player would make 
a CR easier or more difficult, those are resolved with 
applying Boons or Banes to the check. 
Remember,  their  experience  in  the  Skill  is  already 
determined by their Skill Rank so being skilled doesn’t 
justify a lower CR, it is made easier by having a greater 
chance at success
Example (Varying CR) :  The  Party  comes  across  a  wooden 
door that is locked. The door is fairly fragile but still requires 
a bit of force to break, requiring a Tough CR (3) for one of the 
Trainers. He  only  has  an  Athletics Rank  of  Novice  (3 d 6)  so 
he sends out his Machamp to punch a hole through it. The 
Challenge  Rating  is  still  Tough, even  if  the  Machamp  does 
it.  The  Rating  is  dependent  on  how  hard  it  is  to  complete 
the task, regardless of who is doing it. It would be easier for 
the Machamp to accomplish because he has a much higher 
Athletics Rank than his Trainer but it doesn’t mean the CR 
becomes lower when he performs it. 
Example (Applying Context): There are 2 Trainers that both 
have Expert  Stealth and  they’re confronted by  a  high  tech 
padlock.  The  difficulty  of  this  task  would  deem  that  the 
Challenge  Rating  be  Severe  (4).  One  Trainer has  an  Adept 
Tech Edu and has experienced that lock in the past, leading 
to  him  gaining a  Boon  to  the  roll. The  other  Trainer, while 
skilled  at  picking  normal  locks,  has  Pathetic Tech Edu  and 
would have a rough time picking this lock, leading to them 
gaining a Bane to this roll.

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.34)
body:
3434
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
So if your experience in a Skill is determined by your Skill Rank, and Challenge Rating is determined by the inherent 
difficulty of the task, how do you factor in context of who is performing the challenge and what may make it easier or 
harder? This is accomplished with Boons & Banes! 
By default, a Success is a dice that rolled a 4+ (Coined your Success Value). But with Boons & Banes, what determines 
a success is altered. If you have a Boon, the Success Value becomes 3+ . If you have a Bane, the Success Value 
becomes 5+. If a Roll would be affected by a Bane and a Boon, they cancel out one for one.  
Ways to gain Boons

•  Circumstances in the Scene would lead you to have an Advantage

•  Your Personality or Character Qualities would lead you to have an Advantage

•  You’ve passed a Skill Check from this specific task before in the past

•  You invest time into learning about a specific topic
Ways to gain Banes

•  The Check is for a Skill you have a high rank in but aren’t knowledgable in

•  Circumstances in the Scene would lead you to have a Disadvantage

•  Your Personality or Character Qualities would hinder your attempt to do this task
Below are some examples of Scenarios in which a Skill Check would gain a Boon or Bane, with each of the ways above 
listed.
Example (Scene Advantage): A Character is chasing an assailant through a city throughout alleyways. They grew up 
in this city and have the Naturewalk (Urban) so they would know the city like the back of their hand, giving them an 
advantage and a Boon in any related Skill Checks
Example (Quality Advantage): A Character is very timid and tries to socialize with their Ralts, who is also timid. Due 
to their personalities matching they can empathise better and they gain a Boon to their Skill Check for the Downtime 
Action.
Example (Past Check Advantage): A Character has lived with their brother all their life and knows he’s a chronic liar . 
They gain a Boon for an Intuition Check to discern if he’s telling the truth this time. A Character has hacked into a 
computer at a previous team rocket base and is hacking into another that has the same security and is the same type 
of system.
Example (Time Investment): A Player Researches about local mythology in Lumiose City and gains a Boon whenever 
they perform a Skill Check against the creatures they researched about
Example (Skill Disadvantage): A Character is an herbalist that has lived in the City all her life. They have Expert Nature 
Edu but only because they know everything about herbs. When they do a Nature Edu Check for surviving in the wild, 
that isn’t something they’d be an Expert Rank in and they get a Bane. A Character has good Occult Edu for ghost 
knowledge but would know nothing about Ultra Beast Mythology.
Example (Scene Disadvantage): A Character is trying to find a crucial piece of evidence in the office of the mayor . 
They hear someone arrive in the home unexpectedly, causing a panic and rush to find it. They fail their Focus Check 
which would have kept their cool, resulting in a Bane for their Perception Check. 
Example (Quality Disadvantage) : A Character is performing their first concert in a major venue! They’re used to 
smaller crowds and have extreme stage fright. Despite being great at playing music they perform the roll with a Bane 
to account for being nervous.
Boons & Banes

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.35)
body:
3535
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Degrees of Success
So what is the benefit of measuring Skill Checks via Successes instead of adding all the numbers vs a Target Number? 
One major benefit is that it allows you to easily implement variable success levels, allowing the GM to cater the result 
of the Skill Check based on how much you succeeded or failed by. 
When a Skill Check occurs and the Challenge Rating is determined, the GM will have an idea of what happens depending 
on how many successes you exceed or fail by the CR’s Value. The Table below will show what type of result will typically 
happen whenever you pass or fail a Skill Check. Underneath the table will also go over a list of examples and how they 
determine the result. (Failing a Trivial CR Skill Check always results in a Moderate or Critical Failure)
GM Note: Just because a Character rolled a Moderate or Critical Failure doesn’t mean there needs to be penalties 
other than not succeeding. If a Skill Check is low stakes they just get the worst possible outcome, which sometimes 
isn’t that bad! If a Player makes a Skill Check for noticing a tattoo hidden on the forearm of their rival and they have a 
Critical Failure, they simply don’t notice it, nothing bad happens.
Skill Check 
Result
Successes 
Noted Typical Outcome
Critical Failure
2 or less Successes than the CR 
+ more than half of the dice 
resulted in a “1”
They don’t succeed and whatever they tried backfires in 
some way, likely the worst possible outcome
Moderate Failure 2 or less Successes than the CR They don’t succeed in their task and they suffer some 
kind of setback or penalty as a result
Basic Failure 1 less Success than the CR They don’t succeed in their task but they don’t suffer 
any meaningful penalties, trivial if any.
Basic Success Success equals the CR They succeed in their task and get an outcome of what 
was to be expected
Moderate Success 1 Success more than the CR They succeed in their task and the outcome was better 
than expected.
Critical Success 2+ Successes more than the CR
They succeed in their task and the outcome was the 
best they could’ve hoped for, possibly gaining more 
than what they anticipated.
Scenario - James is attempting to cook a lavish meal for a governor as part of a ruse at one of their parties. He needs 
to distract the Mayor while his teammates survey his house. He is impersonating the Governor’s private chef. The 
following is what the GM deems happens on each possible result.
Critical Failure - Though highly, highly improbable, on a Critical Failure, something unexpected happens and 
James sets the timer on for the wrong time, burning the meal and making it unservable. The governor gets 
angry and wants to have a word with his chef…who he doesn’t realize was replaced by James. 
Moderate Failure - James was unfamiliar with the meal he wanted and ended up cooking to the best 
of his ability…which didn’t end well. It was edible but it certainly wasn’t tasty and the governor lost his 
appetite, leaving dinner early and risking his teammates being found out. 
Basic Failure - James ended up cooking the meal, it just wasn’t to his own standard, ruining his 
ego and making the governor slightly suspicious.
Basic Success - James ended up cooking the meal fairly well. The governor ate as normal and 
everything went as planned. 
Moderate Success - The meal was extremely good and the governor was distracted for 
even longer than expected, savoring every bite. 
Critical Success -  The meal was so delicious that the governor was distracted for 
even longer, savoring every bite. He even ignores a security alert from his phone 
because he was enthralled by dinner . When meeting James later, he also gets a 
Boon when lying to the Governor, saying he’s a friend of the chef, because he 
was so good at cooking that the lie is believable.

title: Assistance Modifier can’t be used either
body:
GM Note - As a GM, you may reject any of the following modifiers 
to be applied to a roll. For example, if a situation has little to no 
chance of success such as a bad speech, no amount of exertion will 
allow them to succeed so asking for it should be denied.
If the Players have no way of directly assisting with a check, the 
Assistance Modifier can’t be used either
3636
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Exertion
After you roll a Skill Check, you may declare that you’re 
using the Exertion Modifier . Describe how you overexert 
yourself or put extra effort into this in Character . When 
you do so, and if approved by the GM, reroll the Skill 
Check and take the new result. 
If  you  succeed  on  the  rerolled Skill  Check,  you  suffer 
a Minor Setback. If you fail on the rerolled Skill Check, 
you receive a Major Setback, usually forcing a Critical 
Failure regardless of how much you failed by.
Before you decide to use the Exertion Modifier, the GM 
will tell you the general consequences that may occur 
as a result of it. 
Ex (Describing Consequences): A Character is performing a 
high speed chase in a city, jumping over rooftops in pursuit. 
They  fail  an  Acrobatics  check  when  jumping  over  a  gap 
between buildings and decide to use the Exertion modifier 
so  they  don’t  plummet  to  intense  pain.  The  GM  will  state 
that  if  they  don’t  do  Exertion  they  could  possibly  catch 
something that breaks their fall. However, if they do so, on a 
success they’ll make it to the other side but get injured in the 
process. But if they fail they won’t be able to break their fall 
and will get very much hurt in the process. 
The  Player decides  to  test their  luck  and  rerolls it,  passing 
barely and as they make it to the other side, they lose their 
footing  and  tumble,  gaining  the  Wounded  Affliction  and 
losing 3 Ticks of HP . 
Ex (Light Consequence):   A  Character  isn’t  great  at  being 
stealthy  and  while  traveling  with  the  group  on  a  heist, 
fails  the  check  by  one  success.  They  perform  the  Exertion 
Modifier  to  reroll  and  they  pass.  The  Player  suggests  that 
while they’re focused on being stealthy, they’ll accidentally 
drop a locket of their missing lover and not notice it. Another 
player will have to make a Perception check to notice it.
Ex (Double Failure ):  A  Character  is  making  an  important 
speech. After failing the check and realizing that the crowd 
isn’t  responding  with  enthusiasm,  they  enact  the  Exertion 
Modifier and describe themselves ramping up the energy to 
get the crowd engaged. They Roll once more but fail again. 
The crowd becomes irate at the speech and begin throwing 
harsh words and rotten fruit at the speaker .
Whenever a Pokemon or Trainer would perform a Skill 
Check, either as a Downtime Action or during Narrative 
Play, they can enact  various modifiers listed below in 
order to improve their odds of success.
Assistance
Whenever  a  Skill  Check  would  be  made,  an  ally  may 
assist in the task with GM approval. When they enact 
an Assistance Modifier, they must declare how they’re 
helping and assign a Skill to it. The GM may require a 
Skill Check by the Player to determine if it helps them 
but usually it doesn’t need a check. 
Once  approved,  the  Character  that  is  being  assisted 
will add 1 d 6 to their Die Pool (But cannot exceed 6 d 6). 
If  the  Assisting  Ally  has  at  least  Expert  Rank  in  their 
assigned  Skill,  they  also  apply  a  Boon  to  the  assisted 
Skill Check. An Assisted Skill Check can only be affected 
by one ally, otherwise it becomes a Group Skill Check. 
Ex (Opposing):  Because he failed a Perception Check, James 
didn’t  realize  there  were  2  more  merchants  nearby  that 
were also able to notice a thief attempting to steal from a 
Vendor . He was performing a Stealth Check opposed by the 
Vendor’s Perception, however, now the Vendor gains +1 d 6 
and a Boon due to being assisted by the nearby Merchants. 
Ex (Assisting): James is attempting to pickpocket a merchant 
while  his  friend  is  talking to  them  and  being  a  distraction. 
The friend assigns that they’re assisting with the Command 
Skill to serve as keeping the Vendor’s attention. They have 
Expert Command, which grants James a +1 d 6 to their Stealth 
Check as well as giving him a Boon in it..
Routine
Players  may  enact  the  Routine  Skill  Modifier  when 
they perform a Skill Check that doesn’t have any risk or 
stress attached to it. If that applies, instead of rolling, 
they take half of their Dice Pool (Rounded Down) and 
treat that as the number of successes they got.
Skill Check Modifiers

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.37)
body:
3737
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
37
Full Actions 
Whenever something mentions a Full Action, it requires 
you use both your Standard and Swift Action in order 
to perform it. This can include some Attacks, or strong 
Features. 
Reactions
Reactions  are  an  Action  type  that  are  usually  tied 
to  Features  or  Abilities  that  can  be  Triggered  by  a 
condition occurring. Like other Actions, you only have 
one Reaction per Round for your set of Actions. 
Movement Actions
The  Movement  Action  is  the  most  straightforward 
action; it’s simply used for Movement most of the time. 
You may use Movement Actions to perform any of the 
following: 

•   You may move your Character any number of 
spaces, obeying the following properties:
- You may not exceed your Movement Value in 
spaces moved per Movement Action
 -You may not split up your movement between your 
other Actions - that would require the use of an 
additional Movement Action. (Ex: Move 3, Attack, 
Move 3)

•  Returning a Pokémon, or sending out a 
Pokémon 

•  Returning a Fainted Pokémon and sending out a 
replacement Pokémon

•  Certain Features, Abilities or Combat Maneuvers
Free Actions 
Many  features  or  abilities  can  be  activated  as  Free 
Actions. You can activate as many Free Actions as you 
like  on  your  Turn,  or  once  when  they  are  triggered, 
per resolving instance. Unless they are Triggered, Free 
Actions still can only be used on your Turn and cannot 
be used in the middle of other actions. 
Extended Actions 
Extended  Actions  take  at  least  a  few  minutes  to 
complete,  depending  on  the  task.  If  unspecified, 
assume  at  least  a  few  minutes  with  concentration 
adequate to the task. Simply, these actions cannot be 
performed in the middle of a combat scene.
 
At  the  start of  each  Round,  all  Combatants get  a  set 
of Actions (Max 2 sets of Actions per Player between 
all their controlled Combatants). These Actions can be 
used  when  the  Combatant gains Initiative, or  outside 
of their Turn if it has a Trigger . If a Trainer has multiple 
Pokemon on the Field, they may distribute their second 
set of Actions among their active Pokemon as they see 
fit, with the first set being solely for the Trainer’s Turn. 
A set of Actions consist of the following: 

•  A Standard Action | A Swift Action  
A Movement Action | A Reaction
Note:  Basically, if  you  have one  Pokemon out  and  you are 
participaitng in combat as a trainer, you both get the actions 
above. If you have two Pokemon active on the field, you can 
split the actions from the second set between them. So your 
active Poochyena could move with Movement Action while 
your active Chimchar uses a Standard Action for ember .
Standard Actions 
Attacks and many Features require a Standard Action 
to activate and use. You may use a Standard Action to 
use the following:

•  Using an Attack from your Attack List

•  Using an Item in your Inventory

•  Using some Combat Maneuvers

•  Using some Features or Abilities

•  At any Time, you may use a Standard Action to gain 
an Action below. 
  

•  Swift Action, Reaction or Movement Action. 
Swift Actions 
You may use Swift Actions to perform any of the 
following:

•  Giving an Adjacent Ally an Item from your Inventory 
(Or Switching Items)

•  Equipping or Unequipping an Item from your 
Inventory or Equipment Slots

•  Using some Combat Maneuvers

•  Using Attacks through the Versatile Keyword

•  Using some Features or Abilities

•  Charge a Set-Up Attack

•  Use some Features or Abilities
Action Types

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.38)
body:
3838
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Combat Stats
Speed
Speed Values determine a few things. Every 5 Points a 
Combatant has in Speed, they gain +1 Evasion, up to a 
Maximum of +6. Unlike Special or Physical Evasion, this 
can  be  applied  to  any  opposing  Attacks. Additionally, 
for every 5 Points a Combatant has in Speed, they have 
a +1 Modifier to Initiative Checks.
Temporary Hit Points
Some effects grant Temporary Hit Points which serve as 
a shield and HP Buffer for combatants. If a Pokemon is 
recalled with Temporary HP , it is lost. 
Temporary Hit Points are “bonus” health that stacks on 
top of “real” Hit Points - so you can benefit from gaining 
it  even  if  you  are  already  at  full  health.  However, 
Temporary Hit Points are always lost first from damage 
or  HP  Loss  effects.  Damage  carries  over  directly  to 
real Hit Points once the Temporary Hit Points are lost. 
Furthermore, Temporary Hit  Points do  not  stack with 
other  Temporary Hit  Points  –  only  the  highest  value 
applies.
For example, if you have 10 Temporary Hit Points, and 
then gain 8 Temporary Hit Points - nothing happens. If 
the next turn you were then to gain 15 Temporary Hit 
Points, your  Temporary Hit  Points would  go  up  to  15 
Temporary Hit Points also do not stack with “Real” Hit 
Points for the purposes of determining percentages of 
Hit Points. If a Pokémon has exactly 1 real Hit Point and 
has 50 Temporary Hit Points, they would use the Moves
and effects as if they have 1 Hit Point, not 51.
Glass Cannon Rule
Whenever you level up as a Trainer or Pokemon, you 
can invest Level-Up Points into Stats and grow stronger, 
which is great! But there is one rule you must follow 
when leveling up and investing Points. 
You cannot have more than half of your total gained 
Stat Points invested in one stat.
Note: This rule may be ignored if  you intend to split between 
two stats. Due to the nature of leveling up, if I want to end 
up to 50% in HP and 50% in Speed with no other investment, 
leveling up to level 2 will lead me to have 10 invested in HP 
and  5  in  Speed  which  breaks  this  rule.  However  with  this 
intent in mind, the rule would be resolved next level when 
they put 5 points in speed for 10 in each. Just inform your 
GM first. 
The  idea  of  this  rule  is  basically  to  prevent  people  from 
dumping all their Points into Attack and crumpling if they’re 
attacked even once. Not fun.
Pokemon  Tabletop  Evolution  uses  the  same  Stat 
Concepts similar to the mainline games, however they 
function slightly differently in regards to calculations and 
what they can do in battle. 
These 6 Stats are known as HP , Attack, Special Attack, 
Defense, Special Defense and Speed
HP (Hit Points)
HP  Stat  Values  determine  your  Hit  Points  and  your 
ability  to  take  hits  in  combat  and  remain  conscious. 
If  a  Combatant  would  reach  0  Hit  Points,  they  gain 
the  Fainted Condition  and  are  unable  to  take actions. 
Hit  Points  are  calculated  differently  for  Pokemon  and 
Trainers using the following Equation
Trainer Hit Points - Trainer Level x 5 + (HP x 3) +10
Pokemon Hit Points - Pokemon Level + (HP x 3) +10
Attack
Attack Values determine how hard you can hit Physical 
Attacks. When performing Damage Rolls, you add your 
Attack Value as the Offensive Stat for Physical Category 
Attacks. 
Special Attack
Special  Attack Values determine  how  hard  you  can  hit 
Special  Attacks.  When  performing  Damage  Rolls,  you 
add your Special Attack Value as the Offensive Stat for 
Special Category Attacks. 
Defense
Defense  Values  determine  how  easy  it  is  to  avoid 
Physical  Attacks  and  your  ability  to  endure  damage 
from  Physical  Attacks.  Whenever  a  Combatant  is  hit 
by  a  Physical  Attack,  they  subtract  their  Defense  Stat 
from the damage first before applying Damage to their 
Hit Points. Additionally, for every 5 Points a Combatant 
has  in  Defense, they  gain  +1  Physical Evasion, up  to  a 
Maximum of +6. Evasion gained this way does not apply 
to Special or Status Attacks. 
Special Defense
Special  Defense  Values  determine  how  easy  it  is  to 
avoid Special Attacks and your ability to endure damage 
from Special Attacks. Whenever a Combatant is hit by a 
Special Attack, they subtract their Special Defense Stat 
from the damage first before applying Damage to their 
Hit Points. Additionally, for every 5 Points a Combatant 
has in Special Defense, they gain +1 Special Evasion, up 
to a Maximum of +6. Evasion gained this way does not 
apply to Physical or Status Attacks.

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.39)
body:
3939
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
Critical Hit Range
Critical  Hit  Range,  also  known  as  Crit  Range,  is  a 
modifier that is used to extend the number needed to 
become a Critical Hit. Some Attacks may have a larger 
range at  which  it  can  lead  to  a  Critical Hit,  but most 
are default at a natural 20. You cannot have a Crit 
Range Modifier that exceeds +6. So Leaf Blade with a 
Crit Range of 17+, can never exceed 11+. Sources such 
as  Super  Luck  (Ability)  may improve Crit  Range.  If  an 
Crit Range has a penalty/negative modifier, it adds to 
the Crit Range. For example, a 15+ Crit Range with a -2 
Penalty to Crit Ranges would result in a 17+ Crit Range. 
This  cannot  exceed a  range of  20+  to  result  in  never 
being able to Critical hit.
Evasion
Evasion  is  the  Combat  Value  for  determining  how 
Combatants  can  avoid  Attacks.  There  are  two  types 
of  Evasion,  Specified  and  General.  Specified  Evasion 
only applies to specific types of circumstances. This is 
rare but is primarily in regards to Physical and Special 
evasion, derived from the Defense and Special Defense 
Stat. If  a  Combatant with  4  Physical Evasion is  hit  by 
Confusion,  they  cannot  apply  it  since  the  attack  is 
Special. Then there is General Evasion which is usually 
just  called  Evasion. This  can  be  applied  to  any Attack 
or Maneuver used against you such as from the Speed 
Stat or from outside sources. When Applying Evasion, 
you cannot choose more than one Stat Evasion Value 
to apply and the Evasion cannot exceed a value of 6. 
Example (Low Evasion): A Nidoran has 16 Defense (3 Physical 
Evasion) and 11 Speed (2 Evasion) and 4 Special Defense (0 
Special  Evasion). They’re  hit  by  a  Physical Attack like Horn 
Attack. They  apply  3  Evasion against it  since  it’s a  Physical 
Attack. (They choose Defense as their Stat Evasion to apply 
so they cannot add the 2 Evasion from Speed). If they’re hit 
by a Special Attack like Confusion, they can only apply their 
2 Evasion from Speed. 
Example (Bonus Evasion):   Nidoran  from  the  previous 
example  is  holding  an  Item  that  grants  them  +2  Evasion. 
When  they’re’  hit  by  the  same  Horn  Attack, their  Evasion 
against it  instead becomes  5  because  they  can  add  bonus 
Evasion modifiers to their evasion derived from Stats.
In  addition  to  Combat  Stats,  there  are  other  Values 
that affect Combat in some ways. Most of these values 
can be changed temporarily for a duration in combat 
but some sources may lead to permanent modifiers in 
these categories. 
Note: As a general rule of thumb, Modifier Bonuses cannot 
exceed +6 in value and Penalties to Combat Values cannot 
exceed -6.   If  you  would  have  a  -2  Penalty  to  Accuracy 
but  you’re  already  Blinded  and  have -6,  the -2  is  ignored. 
However  if  you  have  a  positive  modifier  while  exceeding 
this threshold, it does not ignore it. If you have a total of -8 
Accuracy and gain +2, you still have -6 Accuracy. 
 
Accuracy
Accuracy Values are applied to your Accuracy Rolls and 
added  as  a  Modifier . You cannot have an Accuracy 
Value higher than +6 . In addition, Accuracy rolls that 
are modified  by  an  Accuracy value do  not  lead  to an 
Effect Range or  Crit  Range triggering,  as  it  must be  a 
Natural Roll. If an Effect Range is 17+, and you roll a 15 
but have a +3 Accuracy Modifier, the final result is 18, 
but it does not trigger the Effect Range. 
Effect Range
Effect Range Values are modifiers that you may use to 
extend Effect Ranges of Attacks you use. If you have a 
+2 to Effect Ranges, an Attack with a 18+ Effect Range 
to Burn the Target becomes 16+ instead. You cannot 
have an Effect Range Modifier that exceeds +6. So the 
18+ Effect Range can never exceed 12+. Sources such 
as Serene Grace (Ability) may improve Effect Ranges. If 
an Effect Range has a penalty/negative modifier, it adds 
to the Effect Range. For example, a 15+ Effect Range to 
Burn a Target with a -2 Penalty to Effect Ranges would 
result in a 17+ Effect Range. This cannot exceed a range 
of  20+  to  result in  never applying  the  Effect Range  A 
specific Effect Range Modifier always stacks alongside 
generic  modifiers  for  the  sake  of  being  a  maximum 
of  +6.  For  example,  if  Electric  Specialist  increases 
Paralyzed Ranges by +1, they can only benefit from +5 
more Effect Range increases. 
Save Checks
Save  Check  Values  are  applied  to  your  Save  Checks 
whenever  you  roll  them.  These  allow  you  to  cure 
afflictions easier but modifiers gained this way cannot 
exceed +6. 
Combat Values

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.40)

4040
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
40
Movement
Your Movement  Value determines  how  many  spaces 
you can move when using a Movement Action to move. 
By default, all creatures have a Movement Value of 6, 
however this can be changed through other sources or 
Movement  Capabilities.  This  can  also  be  temporarily 
changed during combat.  
Size
Your Size  refers to  how  many  spaces  your  Character 
takes up. This can encompass multiple values such as 
Small (1 x 1), Medium (1 x 1), Large (2 x 2), and Huge 
(3 x 3). 
Carrying Objects
There are three states of carrying objects, Ease, Staggering and Unable. If you’re able to carry an object with Ease, 
there are no issues but you need an empty Weapon Equipment Slot to carry them (Same with Staggering). If you’re 
able to carry it with Staggering,  you’re Vulnerable and Weakened while carrying it and your Movement Value is 
halved, but able to do so. If you’re Unable, you can’t pick up the object at all. 
The Chart below will list what your Power Value needs to be to carry objects depending on their Weight Class. 
WC Power Value for Ease Power Value for Staggering Unable to Carry
1 1+ N/A N/A
2 4+ 3 or Less N/A
3 7+ 4-6 3 or Less
4 10+ 7-9 6 or Less
5 11+ 8-10 7 or Less
6 N/A 11+ 10 or Less
Weight Class
Weight Class Values determine how much an Object or 
Character Weighs. The system rarely references this but 
refer below to see your Weight Class Value. 

• WC 1 (0-25 lb), WC 2 (25-55 lb), WC 3 (55-110 lb), 
WC 4 (110-220 lb), WC 5 (220-440 lb), 
WC 6 (Heavier than 440 lb) 
Power
Power  is  a  rough  estimate  of  a  Character’s  physical 
strength  and  ability  to  lift  heavy  objects.  A  Trainer’s 
Power Value is equal to your Athletics + Combat Rank 
combined (Rounded Up). You cannot have more than 
12 Power.

title: Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE (p.41)
body:
4141
Chapter 3 - Fundamentals of PTE
41
Additionally,  Speed  Combat  Stages  have  a  special 
property about  them. For every 2 Combat Stages in 
Speed, a Character’s Movement Value is adjusted by 
1. For example, if a Combatant has -4 CS in Speed, their 
Movement Value is lowered by -2, resulting in 4 instead 
of the default of 6. If a Combatant has +2 CS in Speed, 
they’ll gain +1, resulting in 7. 
Lastly  regarding  Combat  Stages,  there  is  a  concept 
known  as  Default CS Value.   Whenever  you  enter  a 
Scene, your Combat Stages are reset to their Default CS 
Value, which is almost always at +0 CS! (This prevents 
you from sitting in a tree, swords dancing a couple of 
times then initiating battle) 
However some things refer to increasing your Default 
CS in a Stat. If this occurs, these Combatants will start a 
Scene with higher Combat Stages! When your Default 
CS is adjusted, make sure to note the verbiage used. If 
the Default CS Value is “Set” to a value, it becomes that 
Value, but if the Default CS Value is “Increased” it takes 
the  value  you’re  set  at  and  improves  it.  If  you  have 
your Default CS for Attack set to +1, then an Item that 
increases it by +1, your Default CS Value is now +2 CS. 
Many  Attacks alter  stats  by  raising  or  lowering  their 
Combat Stages (shorthanded to CS) ,  making  them 
either  more  or  less  formidable  respectively.  Only 
Attack,  Defense,  Special  Attack,  Special  Defense  and 
Speed have Combat Stages while HP and Hit Points do 
not have any. 
Attacks  and  Effects  may  alter  Combat  Stages  any 
number of times but they may never be raised higher 
than +6 or lower than -6. For  every  Combat  Stage 
above 0, a Stat is raised by 20%. This means that if a 
Stat has raised 6 CS, its affected Stat should be 220% 
of its original value. For every Combat Stage below , a 
Stat is lowered by 10%. This means that if a Stat has -6 
CS, its affected Stat should be 40% of its original value. 
Consult  the  following chart  to  see  the  multipliers for 
any given Combat Stage. To derive the correct value for 
a given stat, simply multiply it by the multiplier of its 
corresponding Combat Stage.
Combat Stages
CS (Negative) Multiplier
-1 x 0.9
-2 x 0.8
-3 x 0.7
-4 x 0.6
-5 x 0.5
-6 x 0.4
CS (Positive) Multiplier
+1 x 1.2
+2 x 1.4
+3 x 1.6
+4 x 1.8
+5 x 2.0
+6 x 2.2

title: Spirit Points, or SP , is the pseudo equivalent to Action
body:
4242
Spirit Points, or SP , is the pseudo equivalent to Action 
Points (AP) in PTU. 
At the start of each Session, each Trainer and three of 
their Pokemon gain SP equal to their Tier Level. Players 
and  their  Pokemon cannot  have  more  than  6  SP  at  a 
time. The GM may also grant SP to important enemies 
at the start of a Scene equal to double their Tier Level. 
This may include bosses or important characters like a 
rival or gym leader . The only other way of gaining Spirit 
Points is through the Training Downtime Action.
SP can be used for any of the following: 
1. You may expend any number of SP to add a +2 
Uncapped Modifier for each SP expended to an 
Accuracy Roll or Save Check after performing the roll 
and seeing the result. 
Example: Gallade uses Psycho Cut and misses, but spends 2 
SP to add +4 to the result. 
2. You may expend any number of SP to add a +1 d 6 to 
any Skill Check for each SP spent before performing 
the roll. This cannot result in you rolling double or more 
than your original dice pool (Inept cannot be targeted, 
Untrained cannot exceed 3 d 6, Novice Skill cannot 
exceed 5 d 6, etc) 
Example: A Player attempts to convince a merchant to show 
them their secret wares. They’re untrained and spend 1 SP to 
roll 3 d 6. 
3. Some Effects that grant Narrative Utility may utilize 
SP as a resource to either use their effects or improve it 
further, such as Capabilities. 
Example: A Player uses the Illusionist Capability and spends 
1 SP to ignore the sensory input restriction, allowing them to 
create a cake that smells good.

Tier 1 
Tier Level: 1
Tier Value: 5
For Trainers: Trainer Level 1 - 4 is Tier 1
For Pokemon: Pokemon Level 1 - 20 is Tier 1
Tier 2 
Tier Level: 2
Tier Value: 10
For Trainers: Trainer Level 5 - 9 is Tier 2
For Pokemon: Pokemon Level 21 - 49 is Tier 2
Tier 3 
Tier Level: 3
Tier Value: 20
For Trainers: Trainer Level 10+ is Tier 3
For Pokemon: Pokemon Level 50+ is Tier 3
In order for some effects to remain relevant at different 
stages  of  the  game  and  for  combat  values  to  be 
balanced  at  different stages,  some  effects may  scale 
through Level Tiers. If an Effect refers to a Tier Value 
or Tier Level, refer to the number listed under its Tier . 
You can find your current Tier listed in the paragraph 
to the right
Note: Tier Values and Tier Levels are not the same thing
Example 1 :  Anger  Point  grants  a  bonus  to  Damage  Rolls 
equal  to  their  Tier  Value while  Enraged  and  a  Modifier  to 
Critical Hit equal to their Tier Level. 
For  Tier  1,  this  would  be  a  +5  bonus  to  Damage  and  +1 
Modifier to Critical Hits. For Tier 2, this would be a +10 bonus 
to Damage and +2 Modifier to Critical Hits. For Tier 3, this 
would be a +20 bonus to Damage and +3 Modifier to Critical 
Hits. 
Example 2: Effect spore has the Triggering Enemy must pass 
a Standard CR (2) Athletics Check or else they roll a d 3. If the 
user is Tier 2, it becomes a Tough CR (3) Athletics Check. If 
the user is Tier 3, they also have a Bane to the Skill Check.

Static 
Effect: You may qualify for Command Prerequisites as 
if they were Intimidate instead and vice versa. When

Prerequisite: Novice Nature Edu
Static 
Effect: You may craft Simple Poultices. At Expert Rank 
Nature Education, you may craft Greater Poultices.

Prerequisite: You have the Naturewalk Capability
Static 
Effect: Choose a Naturewalk Capability you have. You 
gain a Boon to Skill Checks while in the chosen Terrain 
or involving Pokemon that have that Naturewalk 
Capability. This Boon only applies to Skill Checks 
related to the Terrain, not just being there. This may 
be taken multiple times, choosing a different Terrain

talking to street vendors or Intuition Check for knowing

Prerequisite: Novice Athletics or Focus
Static 
Effect: You may craft Crude Armor. At Expert Rank of 
your qualifying Skill, you may craft Light Armor. At 
Master Rank you may craft Heavy Armor and if you 
have Adept Rank Occult Edu, you may also craft Arcane

Prerequisite: Novice Command or Intimidate

Effect: Whenever you Train or Socialize Pokemon that

Caravanner
Prerequisite: Novice Athletics
Static 
Effect: While you are on an Average or Long Journey, 
[Large] Items in your Inventory (Not Equipment) are 
treated as only taking 1 Slot instead of 2. 
Confident
Prerequisite: Novice Command
Static 
Effect: Whenever you perform a Charm, Guile or 
Intimidate Skill check, add +1 d 6 to the roll. If that Skill 
Rank is equal to or higher than your Command Rank, 
you instead treat any results of 5 as if you rolled a 6. 
 
When you Level-Up, you may also choose to gain Effects known as Talents instead of ranking up a skill. This allows 
your Trainer to gain special perks that either minorly affect combat or primarily serve as narrative or out of combat 
tools. If you create homebrew Talents, be sure to make it something that can’t be done with a normal Skill Check, 
such as the ability to identify poisonous mushrooms.

Skill Specialty
Prerequisite: A Novice Skill
Static 
Effect: Choose a Specialty based on one of your qualifying 
Skills. Whenever you would perform a Skill Check that is 
related to your Specialty, add 1 d 6 to the roll (This may exceed 
6 d 6). If your Specialty is deemed to be Niche in application 
(GM Discretion), you may instead take two Niche Specialties. 
You may take this Talent multiple times. 
GM Note: Below is a list of pre approved Specialties for 
each Skill they could qualify in. When they take this Talent, 
negotiate with your player to ensure that their Specialty 
isn’t too generic so it would cover a large portion of related 
Skill Checks. As an example, Lying to Authorities is fine but a 
Specialty of just Lying isn’t because that’s a widespread usage 
of the Skill. Also, the Effect applies to all Skill Checks related to 
that Specialty, not being tied to the qualifying skill only.

Athletics Rank instead of both your Athletics and 
Combat Rank.

Research Downtime Action, after the Skill Check, add a 
modifier to the result equal to three times the number 
of dice that resulted in a 4 or higher. (If you rolled a 
3 d 6 and the result was 3,5,1, the final result will be 12, 
as you are adding +3 from the ‘5’ result) 
Scout
Prerequisite: Expert Nature Edu or Perception
Static 
Effect: Whenever your GM performs a Travel Check 
during a Journey, they must inform you if a result of 
9 or less was rolled. You then gain some information 
about what the Travel Check will result in before your 
group encounters it. Instead of Encountering it, your 
group may decide to avoid it, requiring a Skill Check 
or penalty of some sort, then the Travel Check will be 
resolved. The difficulty or penalty will depend on what 
the Travel Check resulted in.
Scavenger
Prerequisite: Novice Nature Edu or Perception
Static 
Effect: Whenever you perform the Exploration 
Downtime Action, roll a d 20 Luck Roll. On a 6 or less 
you find nothing. On a 7-12 you find something worth 
$500 or less. On a 13-18 you find something worth 
$1,000 or less. On a 19+ you find something worth 
$2,000 or less. As a GM you may determine when this 
Talent is applicable and what they may find depending 
on their Environment, such as finding spare cash 
in a city.
GM Note: Just ban this Talent if you would find this 
tedious. 
Note -  This information could be seeing a massive Nidoking in the 
distance or hearing crackling thunder of an approaching storm 
or just an ominous feeling of something up ahead. The clarity of 
information depends on what was rolled. The penalty or difficulty 
of the Skill Check also depends on what’s rolled. For example, 
running into the Guardian Mandibuzz of the forest may require a 
lot of time to figure out a safe route through the forest, taking the 
entire Afternoon Time Phase but letting them avoid it.

title: Chapter 4 - Trainer Classes
body:
5151
Chapter 4 - Trainer Classes
Base vs Advanced Classes
When categorizing Classes, we have [ Base] Classes 
and [Advanced] Classes. If you take a Base Class, you’ll 
tend to get generic Features that anyone who wants to 
pursue that playstyle will benefit from.
If you take the Defender Class, it’ll give a lot of generic 
tanking and defensive support, however its Advanced 
Classes are all more specific in what they grant based 
off of the direction of “Tank” they want to be. 
Choosing Classes
When deciding on the Classes you’ll take, there are a 
few essential questions you should ask, listed below:
1. Is there going to be Trainer Combat?
If the GM says there is going to be “Direct” Trainer 
combat, you need to be able to do something to 
contribute to Combat. The easiest way to do so is take 
a Class or Features that provide Damage. 
PTE however is built in a way that no matter what 
classes you decide on, you’ll always have something 
of value in combat, but just keep your actions in mind 
when deciding on Classes. 
More importantly, if there is no Trainer Combat, you 
likely should only take Classes in “Pokemon Classes”
2. What is your primary Trainer Identity?
Whatever their identity is, you should usually take the 
Base Class and one of its Advanced Classes so it’ll be 
an easy decision. Are you a Trainer who’s a Water Type 
Gym Leader? Take Type Specialist, Water Specialist 
and maybe a few Pokemon Classes here and there. 
In Base PTE, There are three categories of Classes 
that we have created when designing them originally, 
all of which are listed below 
Pokemon Classes
These Classes are all known as Pokemon Support. 
Features granted in these classes are designed to 
power up your Pokemon, rather than you or they’re 
centered around interacting with Pokemon. 
The Base Classes in this category are Commander, 
Training Specialist, Ranger and Type Specialist. 
Education Classes
These Classes are a mixed bag of Features that benefit 
your Pokemon and benefit yourself, however it leans 
more towards Combat Classes. However, these are 
mainly separated by them all needing Education Skills 
to qualify for them. 
The Base Classes in this category are General 
Researcher, Medicine Researcher, Nature Researcher, 
Occult Researcher, Pokemon Researcher, Performer 
and Tech Researcher.
Combat Classes
These Classes are all known as Trainer Support or 
Direct Combat Classes . Conversely to Pokemon 
Classes, these Classes power up you instead of your 
Pokemon. These Classes tend to provide you with 
Attacks and ways to contribute to battle. You’ll find 
that these Classes tend to align more with traditional 
RPG Roles!
The Base Classes in this category are Fighter, Defender, 
Marksman, Strider, Rogue and Provocateur.
Types of Classes
Features that share a common identity and help a 
Trainer fulfill an archetype mechanically. If you take 
the Defender Class, Features residing under it are all 
defensive options that help your Character tank better . 
As iterated earlier, the only limitation is that you 
can only have up to 4 Classes in total. This means 
that you cannot have more than 4 Features with the 
[Class] Feature Tag. (And considering you can’t qualify 
for the rest of the class without the [Class] Feature, 
you can’t take the class) 
The last aspect of a Trainer that can affect how they 
function in battle are known as Trainer Classes. 
While Classes may be a familiar term to you, unlike 
other TTRPGs, PTU and by extension, PTE are more 
“Classless” in their scope. 
This means that while there are classes, you’re not 
limited to one or two and multiclassing is the norm, 
and in fact, expected of all Trainer Builds. The limit 
of 4 Classes is primarily for the sake of filling out the 
number of Features you would get when leveling up 
and it being the optimal amount of classes needed 
without sacrificing your Trainer’s identity.
Functionally speaking, Classes are simply groups of 
Trainer Classes

Chapter 4 - Trainer Classes
STRATEGIST
Trainers who are strategists go beyond the level of commanders, 
preferring field wide tactics and excelling and commanding multiple 
allies at the same time. Not only that, they can adapt to enemy tactics 
with Protocols or Tactics of their own to counter any strategy they have.
Strategist
[Advanced] [Class] 
Prerequisite 1: Commander [or]
Prerequisite 2: Adept Command and Novice Focus
At-Will - Free Action
Trigger: A Round Starts
Effect: Create a 3 x 3 Observation Zone on the Field that lasts 
until the end of the Round. You may use Basic Orders on 
Allies within this Zone as a Free Action. A Combatant can only 
be affected by an Order used this way once per Round. 
Bonus: You gain the Battle Commander General Feature, 
ignoring Prerequisites
Initiate Protocol
[Order]
Prerequisite: Strategist, Novice Command or Focus
At-Will - Swift Action 
Target: An Ally within 5 m
Effect: Choose a Protocol listed below to apply to 
the Target. Modifiers and Bonuses gained this way 
last until the end of the Round. A Target can only be 
affected by one Protocol at a time and it does not 
stack. X is equal to your Tier Value and Y is equal to 
your Tier Level.

• Protocol - Offense: The Target has a +X Bonus to 
Damage Rolls and +Y to Critical Hit Ranges.

• Protocol - Defense: The Target gains +X Damage 
Reduction and a Tick of Temporary Hit Points

• Protocol - Inspire: The Target has a +Y Modifier to 
Accuracy Rolls and Effect Ranges.

• Protocol - Recover: The Target has +Y Bonus to Save 
Checks and restores a Tick of Hit Points
Personal Instruction
Prerequisite: Strategist, 2 Strategist Features, 
Expert Command or Focus
Static 
Effect: You learn the Attacks Coaching and Instruct. 
When using either of these Attacks, their Range is 
also treated as 6, 1 Target. 
Adaptive Tactics
Prerequisite: Strategist, Adept Command or Focus
At-Will - Standard Action 
Condition: You’re not affected by a Mental Status Affliction 
and there is an Observation Zone on the field
Effect: Choose one of the following to Apply to all Allied 
Combatants within your Observation Zone (And yourself if 
you’re in the Zone):

• Bolstering Tactics: All affected Combatants have all negative 
Combat Stages reset to their Default Value and cannot lose 
Combat Stages until the end of the next Round.

• Breaching Tactics: All affected Combatants have their 
next Damaging Attack that hits be unable to be resisted and 
cannot Trigger Defensive Abilities.

• Fortified Tactics: All affected Combatants resist the next 
Damaging Attack that hits them.

• Recovery Tactics: All affected Combatants pass their next 
Save Check and cannot gain Status Afflictions until the end of 
the next Round.
Field Commander
Prerequisite: Strategist, 3 Strategist Features, 
Master Command or Focus
Scene x 2 - Reaction
Trigger: An Ally or Enemy within your Observation Zone is 
Attacked
Effect: If the Target of the Triggering Attack is an Ally, the 
Attack misses all Allies within your Observation Zone. If the 
Target of the Triggering Attack is an Enemy, the Attack gains 
the Sureshot Keyword. Once per Scene, if the Triggering 
Attacker is also within your Observation Zone, this Feature’s 
Frequency is not expended.
